chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Said from Ibn Mahbub from Abu Hamzah said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about in what amount the thief's hand is cut off. He gathered his two palms and then said: 'In the number of them [the dirhams].' This does not contradict the earlier narrations, which state that the minimum amount in which the thief's hand is cut off is one-quarter of a dinar, for two reasons: One is that it is not impossible that the value of the dirhams he indicated was one-quarter of a dinar, and Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) clarified this in the narration of Muhammad ibn Muslim, which we mentioned at the beginning of the chapter, when he was asked about one who stole two dirhams, and he said: 'In one-quarter of a dinar, whatever the value of the dinar has reached.' The other reason is that we may attribute it to taqiyya (dissimulation), because it is the view of some of the Sunnis.

key_terms.الْعَامَّةِ: The general public (often referring to Sunni Muslims in Shia texts)
key_terms.رُبُعُ دِينَارٍ: One-quarter of a dinar (a standard measure of value)
key_terms.يُقْطَعُ السَّارِقُ: The thief is cut (referring to amputation of the hand)

ai.seo_question: What is the minimum value of stolen goods that requires cutting the thief's hand in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the minimum threshold for hadd al-sariqa by linking the number of dirhams to their monetary value, offering two scholarly interpretations: either the dirhams' value equaled a quarter dinar, or the count was based on taqiyya to align with Sunni jurisprudence. This highlights the dynamic nature of fiqh principles in Shia tradition, where economic context and doctrinal prudence shape legal rulings.
